books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: “Caution!! Colored people of Boston, one & all,” broadside, April 24, 1851

stimulus.source_note: “Caution!! Colored people of Boston, one & all,” broadside posted in Boston, April 24, 1851 (Library of Congress, Printed Ephemera Collection). Public domain.
stimulus.text: Caution!! Colored people of Boston, one & all, You are hereby respectfully cautioned and advised, to avoid conversing with the Watchmen and Police Officers of Boston, For since the recent Order of the Mayor & Aldermen, they are empowered to act as Kidnappers and Slave Catchers, And they have already been actually employed in Kidnapping, Catching, and Keeping Slaves. Therefore, if you value your Liberty, and the Welfare of the Fugitives among you, Shun them in every possible manner, as so many Hounds on the track of the most unfortunate of your race. Keep a Sharp Look Out for Kidnappers, and have Top Eye open. April 24, 1851.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The broadside calls the police “Hounds on the track of the most unfortunate of your race.” That language most directly shows that its authors wanted readers to

options.text: trust the police to tell runaways from free citizens.
options.misconception: The broadside says the opposite: avoid the police entirely, because they have “already been actually employed in Kidnapping, Catching, and Keeping Slaves.”

options.text: leave Boston and settle in the Southern states.
options.misconception: The broadside tells readers to shun the police, not to leave Boston for the South — the South is where the slave catchers would take them.

options.text: petition Congress to extend the Fugitive Slave Act.
options.misconception: The broadside attacks the law's enforcement, it does not ask Congress to extend the law; its authors wanted the law resisted, not strengthened.

options.text: see the police as hunters, not protectors.

rationales.A: The broadside says the opposite: avoid the police entirely, because they have “already been actually employed in Kidnapping, Catching, and Keeping Slaves.”
rationales.B: The broadside tells readers to shun the police, not to leave Boston for the South — the South is where the slave catchers would take them.
rationales.C: The broadside attacks the law's enforcement, it does not ask Congress to extend the law; its authors wanted the law resisted, not strengthened.
rationales.D: Calling officers “Hounds on the track” turns a routine encounter into a hunt, and the broadside's advice follows: “Shun them in every possible manner” and “Keep a Sharp Look Out.”
rationales.general:
1. Hear the image: not officers, but hounds, on the track of the most unfortunate.
2. Ask what a hound does: it hunts by scent, and it does not ask questions first.
3. Follow the image to the advice: shun them in every possible manner, and keep a sharp lookout.
Remember: metaphors in a warning are instructions in disguise — the image tells you how to act.
